n: Love comes first, and obedience flows from it. Moses links loving God with keeping every part of his law, not just on special days but always.

f.g: Charge = the duties or responsibilities God has entrusted to you.

n: Moses speaks to the people who personally lived through these events as youths. They can’t claim ignorance; they have firsthand experience of God’s discipline and power.

f.g: Correction or training, the way a parent disciplines a child (Deuteronomy 8:5).

f.w: his mighty hand, and his stretched out arm

n: He lists what they saw: the signs and plagues that God sent against Pharaoh and the whole land of Egypt.
The great rescue at the Red Sea: the most powerful army of the day was swept away by the returning waters. Egypt’s chariot force never threatened Israel again.

f.w: the water of the Red sea to overflow them

n: God’s care did not stop at the sea. Through forty years of wilderness he fed, led, and corrected them until they reached the plains of Moab.

f.w: what he did unto you in the wilderness

n: A sobering memory: Dathan and Abiram rebelled against Moses’ leadership, and the earth opened and swallowed them. Rebellion against God’s appointed order has consequences.
The point of the list: “you saw it all yourselves.” Personal witness brings personal accountability.
Obedience is the source of strength. Keeping the commandments is what will make Israel able to enter and hold the land.
Long life in the land is tied to faithfulness. The land’s richness is pictured as flowing milk (from flocks) and honey (from bees or date syrup).

f.w: a land that floweth with milk and honey

n: In Egypt, crops depended on Nile irrigation; farmers moved water through channels, possibly opening and closing them with their feet or working foot-driven water wheels.

f.g: Likely refers to opening irrigation ditches with the foot or treading a water wheel.

n: Canaan is hilly, with no great river to rely on. Its life depends on rain — and so on God. This land would teach Israel daily trust.

f.w: drinketh water of the rain of heaven

n: A tender picture: God personally watches over this land all year long, from planting to harvest.

f.w: the eyes of the LORD thy God are always upon it

n: Here begins a passage later recited daily by Jews as part of the Shema prayer. The condition is wholehearted love and service.

f.w: with all your heart and with all your soul

n: Israel’s farming depended on two rainy seasons: the early rains of autumn that softened the ground for planting and the late rains of spring that filled out the grain.

f.w: the first rain and the latter rain

f.g: In KJV English, “corn” means grain such as wheat or barley.

n: God promises pasture for the animals and plenty for the people — blessings for the whole household.

f.w: that thou mayest eat and be full

n: The danger is subtle: a deceived heart. Prosperity can quietly lead people to trust other gods instead of the one who gave the blessings.

f.w: that your heart be not deceived

n: If Israel turned to idols, God would “shut up the heaven” — drought would follow. Elijah’s later drought fulfilled this warning.

f.w: he shut up the heaven, that there be no rain

n: God’s words must be stored inside and worn outside. Later Jews took the hand and forehead language literally with small leather boxes called tefillin.

f.g: Headbands or forehead markers; Jewish practice uses phylacteries (tefillin).

n: Parents are the first teachers. Gospel conversation belongs in everyday life — at home, on walks, at bedtime, and in the morning.

f.w: ye shall teach them your children

n: Writing God’s words on doorposts made every home a reminder of the covenant. Jewish homes still fix a small scroll, the mezuzah, to their doorframes.

f.g: Hebrew mezuzot; the source of the Jewish mezuzah.

n: The reward is a long, settled life in the land for generation after generation — “heaven on earth” for as long as the sky stands.

f.w: as the days of heaven upon the earth
f.g: An idiom for “as long as the heavens last” — permanently.

n: The conditions restated: diligent obedience, love, walking in God’s ways, and clinging to him.
With God fighting for them, Israel would overcome nations larger and stronger than itself.

f.w: greater nations and mightier than yourselves

n: The ideal borders of the promise stretch from the southern desert to Lebanon, and from the Euphrates to the Mediterranean. They were most nearly reached under David and Solomon.

f.w: Every place whereon the soles of your feet shall tread

f.g: In KJV English, “coast” means border or territory.

n: God would go ahead of them, filling their enemies with dread. Rahab later describes exactly this fear in Jericho.

f.w: the fear of you and the dread of you

n: Here is the great choice of Deuteronomy. God lays out two paths and lets Israel decide.
Blessing follows obedience. Agency is real, and so are its results.
The curse follows turning aside to follow gods they had never known — gods that had done nothing for them.

f.g: Gods with no history of saving Israel, unlike the Lord.

n: Once in the land, Israel was to hold a ceremony on two mountains facing each other near Shechem, declaring blessings from one and curses from the other.

f.w: mount Gerizim, and the curse upon mount Ebal

n: Moses gives directions: the mountains lie west of the Jordan in central Canaan, near the oaks of Moreh where Abraham first built an altar in the land.
A confident promise: they will cross the Jordan, take the land, and live there.
The section closes the way it began — with a call to careful obedience. This prepares for the detailed laws starting in chapter 12.

f.g: A Hebrew idiom: “be careful to do.”
